deck.section_name: 13. An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry
deck.title: Isomerism: Structural Isomerism & Stereoisomerism

front_blocks.md: Define **structural isomers**.

back_blocks.md: **Structural isomers** are compounds that have the same **molecular formula** but different **structural formulae**.

cards.front_md: Define **structural isomers**.
cards.back_md: **Structural isomers** are compounds that have the same **molecular formula** but different **structural formulae**.

front_blocks.md: What are the three types of structural isomerism?

back_blocks.md: The three types are **chain isomerism**, **positional isomerism** and **functional group isomerism**.

cards.front_md: What are the three types of structural isomerism?
cards.back_md: The three types are **chain isomerism**, **positional isomerism** and **functional group isomerism**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Propene and cyclopropane are structural isomers.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Both have molecular formula **C**<sub>**3**</sub>**H**<sub>**6**</sub> but different structural formulae. Propene has a C=C double bond while cyclopropane has a ring of three carbon atoms.

front_blocks.md: Define **chain isomerism**.

back_blocks.md: **Chain isomerism** is a type of structural isomerism in which compounds have the same molecular formula but different lengths of the longest carbon chain, caused by **branching**.

cards.front_md: Define **chain isomerism**.
cards.back_md: **Chain isomerism** is a type of structural isomerism in which compounds have the same molecular formula but different lengths of the longest carbon chain, caused by **branching**.

front_blocks.md: Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol are **..........**  isomers because they have the same molecular formula but differ in the **..........**  of the hydroxyl functional group.

back_blocks.md: Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol are **positional** isomers because they have the same molecular formula but differ in the **position** of the hydroxyl functional group.

front_blocks.md: Why do functional group isomers have very different chemical properties, even though they share the same molecular formula?

back_blocks.md: Functional group isomers contain **different functional groups**, which determine the chemical reactivity of the molecule. Different functional groups react by different mechanisms and with different reagents.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are positional isomers.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are **chain isomers**. They share molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> but differ in the length of the longest carbon chain, not in the position of a functional group.

front_blocks.md: What causes chain isomerism to arise?

back_blocks.md: Chain isomerism arises from **branching** in the carbon skeleton, which changes the length of the longest chain even though the molecular formula remains the same.

front_blocks.md: Define **stereoisomers**.

back_blocks.md: **Stereoisomers** are compounds with the same atoms connected to each other in the same order but with those atoms **differently arranged in space**.

cards.front_md: Define **stereoisomers**.
cards.back_md: **Stereoisomers** are compounds with the same atoms connected to each other in the same order but with those atoms **differently arranged in space**.

front_blocks.md: What are the two types of stereoisomerism?

back_blocks.md: The two types are **geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism** and **optical isomerism**.

cards.front_md: What are the two types of stereoisomerism?
cards.back_md: The two types are **geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism** and **optical isomerism**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In a cis isomer, the two identical functional groups are on opposite sides of the double bond.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
In a **cis** isomer, identical functional groups are on the **same side** of the double bond. In a **trans** isomer, they are on opposite sides.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

cards.back_md:
**False.**

In a **cis** isomer, identical functional groups are on the **same side** of the double bond. In a **trans** isomer, they are on opposite sides.

front_blocks.md: Define **enantiomers**.

back_blocks.md: **Enantiomers** are the two optical isomers of a chiral molecule. They are **non-superimposable mirror images** of each other.

cards.front_md: Define **enantiomers**.
cards.back_md: **Enantiomers** are the two optical isomers of a chiral molecule. They are **non-superimposable mirror images** of each other.

front_blocks.md: Geometrical isomerism in alkenes arises because the **..........**  bond prevents **..........**  rotation about the C=C bond, fixing the groups in position.

back_blocks.md: Geometrical isomerism in alkenes arises because the **π** bond prevents **free** rotation about the C=C bond, fixing the groups in position.

cards.front_md: Geometrical isomerism in alkenes arises because the **..........**  bond prevents **..........**  rotation about the C=C bond, fixing the groups in position.
cards.back_md: Geometrical isomerism in alkenes arises because the **π** bond prevents **free** rotation about the C=C bond, fixing the groups in position.

front_blocks.md: How do enantiomers differ from each other in their interaction with polarised light?

back_blocks.md: One enantiomer rotates the plane of polarised light **clockwise** and the other rotates it **anticlockwise**. They rotate it by the same angle but in opposite directions.

cards.front_md: How do enantiomers differ from each other in their interaction with polarised light?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Geometrical isomerism can occur in cyclic compounds as well as in alkenes.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
In cyclic compounds, limited rotation about the C–C bonds that make up the ring fixes substituents either above or below the ring, giving rise to cis/trans **geometrical isomers**.

cards.front_md:

front_blocks.md: Geometrical and optical isomers are both types of **..........**  isomerism. They differ from **..........**  isomers, which have different structural formulae.

back_blocks.md: Geometrical and optical isomers are both types of **stereo** isomerism. They differ from **structural** isomers, which have different structural formulae.

front_blocks.md: Why does free rotation about a C=C double bond not occur, but free rotation about a C–C single bond does?

back_blocks.md: Rotation about a C=C bond would break the **π bond** (which requires energy to re-form), so it does not occur freely. A C–C single bond has only a **σ bond**, which allows free rotation.

cards.front_md: Why does free rotation about a C=C double bond not occur, but free rotation about a C–C single bond does?
cards.back_md: Rotation about a C=C bond would break the **π bond** (which requires energy to re-form), so it does not occur freely. A C–C single bond has only a **σ bond**, which allows free rotation.

front_blocks.md: Define **chiral centre**.

back_blocks.md: A **chiral centre** is a carbon atom bonded to **four different** atoms or groups of atoms, giving rise to two non-superimposable mirror image optical isomers.

cards.front_md: Define **chiral centre**.
cards.back_md: A **chiral centre** is a carbon atom bonded to **four different** atoms or groups of atoms, giving rise to two non-superimposable mirror image optical isomers.

front_blocks.md: How many optical isomers can a molecule with two chiral centres form?

back_blocks.md: A molecule with two chiral centres can form up to **four** optical isomers (2<sup>2</sup> = 4). The maximum number of stereoisomers is **2**<sup>**n**</sup>, where n is the number of chiral centres.

cards.front_md: How many optical isomers can a molecule with two chiral centres form?
cards.back_md: A molecule with two chiral centres can form up to **four** optical isomers (2<sup>2</sup> = 4). The maximum number of stereoisomers is **2**<sup>**n**</sup>, where n is the number of chiral centres.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Enantiomers are superimposable mirror images of each other.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Enantiomers are **non-superimposable** mirror images. Just as a left hand cannot be placed exactly over a right hand, one enantiomer cannot be superimposed on the other.

cards.front_md:

front_blocks.md: Define **chiral molecule**.

back_blocks.md: A **chiral molecule** is a molecule that contains one or more chiral centres and therefore exists as two non-superimposable mirror image forms (enantiomers).

cards.front_md: Define **chiral molecule**.

front_blocks.md: The maximum number of stereoisomers for a molecule with n chiral centres is **..........** . A molecule with three chiral centres can have a maximum of **..........**  stereoisomers.

back_blocks.md: The maximum number of stereoisomers for a molecule with n chiral centres is **2****<sup>n</sup>**. A molecule with three chiral centres can have a maximum of **eight** stereoisomers.

cards.front_md: The maximum number of stereoisomers for a molecule with n chiral centres is **..........** . A molecule with three chiral centres can have a maximum of **..........**  stereoisomers.

front_blocks.md: How do you identify a chiral centre in a cyclic molecule?

back_blocks.md: Find the carbon atom in the ring that is bonded to **four different** atoms or groups of atoms. The two ring bonds count as different groups if the atoms on each side of the ring differ.

cards.front_md: How do you identify a chiral centre in a cyclic molecule?
cards.back_md: Find the carbon atom in the ring that is bonded to **four different** atoms or groups of atoms. The two ring bonds count as different groups if the atoms on each side of the ring differ.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A molecule with one chiral centre always produces exactly two optical isomers.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
One chiral centre gives 2<sup>1</sup> = **two** optical isomers (enantiomers), which are mirror images of each other.

back_blocks.md: To identify a chiral centre, look for a carbon bonded to **four** different atoms or groups. Such a molecule is described as **chiral** and has no plane of symmetry.

front_blocks.md: What is the key condition for geometrical isomerism to occur in a molecule?

back_blocks.md: Geometrical isomerism requires **restricted rotation** about a C–C bond (as in alkenes or cyclic compounds) AND **different groups** attached to each carbon of the restricted bond.

cards.front_md: What is the key condition for geometrical isomerism to occur in a molecule?

front_blocks.md: What is the systematic approach for deducing all possible isomers of an organic compound?

back_blocks.md:
1. Draw the structural formula.
2. Decide whether **stereoisomerism** or **structural isomerism** applies.
3. For structural isomers, check for **chain**, **positional** and **functional group** types. For stereoisomers, check for **geometrical (cis/trans)** and **optical** types.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> has only one possible structural isomer.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> has **two** structural isomers: **butane** (straight chain) and **2-methylpropane** (branched chain). These are chain isomers.

front_blocks.md: Define **positional isomer**.

back_blocks.md: A **positional isomer** is a structural isomer in which the same functional group is located on a **different carbon** of the same parent chain.

cards.front_md: Define **positional isomer**.
cards.back_md: A **positional isomer** is a structural isomer in which the same functional group is located on a **different carbon** of the same parent chain.

front_blocks.md: How many structural isomers does C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>Br<sub>2</sub> (dibromopropane) have and what type of isomerism do they show?

back_blocks.md: Dibromopropane has **four** structural isomers: 1,1-dibromopropane, 2,2-dibromopropane, 1,2-dibromopropane and 1,3-dibromopropane. These are all **positional** isomers.

front_blocks.md: 1,1-dichloroethene is a **..........**  isomer of 1,2-dichloroethene. However, only **..........**  exhibits geometrical isomerism because it has restricted rotation and two different groups on each C=C carbon.

back_blocks.md: 1,1-dichloroethene is a **structural** isomer of 1,2-dichloroethene. However, only **1,2-dichloroethene** exhibits geometrical isomerism because it has restricted rotation and two different groups on each C=C carbon.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A compound with no restricted bond rotation and no chiral centre can exhibit stereoisomerism.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Stereoisomerism requires either **restricted rotation** (for geometrical isomers) or a **chiral centre** (for optical isomers). Without either, only structural isomers are possible.

front_blocks.md: To deduce if geometrical isomerism is possible, first check for **..........**  rotation about a C=C or ring bond, then check that each carbon of the double bond has **..........**  groups attached.

back_blocks.md: To deduce if geometrical isomerism is possible, first check for **restricted** rotation about a C=C or ring bond, then check that each carbon of the double bond has **two different** groups attached.

front_blocks.md: What two conditions must both be met for a molecule to show geometrical isomerism?

back_blocks.md:
1. There must be **restricted rotation** about a C=C bond or within a ring.
2. Each carbon involved in the restricted bond must have **two different groups** attached.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Chain isomerism arises when the same molecular formula can give molecules with different numbers of carbons in the longest chain.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
**Chain isomers** have the same molecular formula but different carbon chain lengths due to branching. For example, butane and 2-methylpropane are both C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>.
